title: Scientists Listen to Roars to Help Protect Wild Animals
summary:
Animals make lots of sounds. They call to find mates, protect their homes or warn others. Scientists can record these sounds to learn which animals live in a place and how many there are. This science is called bioacoustics.

Jonathan Growcott is a biologist who studies big meat-eating animals. Finding them in the wild is hard. So he decided to listen for them. His team put 50 sound recorders in Nyerere National Park in Tanzania, in Africa.

First he studied leopards. Their deep roars sound like sawing wood. A computer model could tell leopards apart by their roars 93 percent of the time.

Then he studied lions. Using artificial intelligence, he found lions make two kinds of roars. He also built a tool he calls "Shazam for lions." It could identify a single lion by its roar more than 95 percent of the time.
why_it_matters: Listening to animals can help scientists protect wildlife that kids love, like lions and leopards.
